nameStory: The 'button' in this lichen's name comes from its small, dark, button-like reproductive structures called apothecia that dot its surface like tiny black buttons sewn onto fabric. These round, raised spots are so distinctive that they've given their name to the entire genus Buellia, making this the 'common' representative of the button lichen family.
description: Common Button Lichen is a crusty, flat lichen that grows directly on tree bark, forming patches that can be gray to brownish in color. It's what scientists call a 'crustose' lichen, meaning it forms a thin crust that's tightly attached to its host surface. The most noticeable features are its small, dark, button-like structures (apothecia) that contain spores for reproduction. Individual patches are usually just a few inches across, but multiple colonies can cover larger areas of bark.

idTips.label: Button-like structures
idTips.description: Look for small, black, round, raised spots scattered across the lichen's surface - these feel slightly bumpy to the touch and look like tiny buttons pressed into the bark

idTips.label: Crusty texture
idTips.description: The lichen forms a thin, flat crust that feels rough and papery when dry, almost like dried paint that's firmly stuck to the bark

idTips.label: Gray to brownish color
idTips.description: The main body appears grayish to light brown, sometimes with a slightly powdery or dusty appearance that may rub off on your fingers

idTips.label: Bark preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on bark rather than rock, with a strong preference for acidic-barked trees like oaks and pines

idTips.label: Patch formation
idTips.description: Forms irregular patches that can merge together, creating a mosaic-like pattern on tree trunks with clearly defined edges

habitat: In New England, you'll find Common Button Lichen on the bark of oak, pine, and juniper trees, especially those with naturally acidic bark. It thrives in higher elevation forests, particularly in the White Mountains and Green Mountains between 2,000-9,800 feet, favoring the cooler, moister conditions of submontane to subalpine forests. Look for it in mixed coniferous and deciduous forests where the air quality is good and humidity levels are consistent.

seasonality.spring: The lichen becomes more noticeable as snow melts and bark dries out, with the dark button structures standing out clearly against the lighter bark. This is an excellent time to spot it as deciduous trees are still bare.
seasonality.summer: Growth is most active during humid summer months, though changes are subtle and slow. The lichen may appear slightly more vibrant in color during periods of consistent moisture.
seasonality.fall: Another prime viewing season as leaves drop and expose more bark surface. The contrast between the lichen and autumn-colored bark makes identification easier.
seasonality.winter: Still visible and identifiable on snow-free bark, though the lichen enters a dormant state. The button-like structures remain the key identifying feature even in harsh winter conditions.

funFact: This lichen is essentially two organisms living as one - a fungus providing structure and protection while tiny algae living inside create food through photosynthesis, making it one of nature's most successful partnerships that can survive freezing temperatures, drought, and even brief trips to space!
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with other crusty lichens on bark, but remember 'buttons on bark' - those distinctive dark, round, raised apothecia are your best clue. Other bark lichens might be crusty too, but they won't have these prominent button-like structures.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'lichen' is often mispronounced - it's 'LIE-ken' not 'LITCH-en.' Many people don't realize that lichens aren't plants at all, but rather a symbiotic partnership between fungi and algae, representing one of evolution's most successful collaborations.
compareHints: Common Button Lichen differs from its Buellia relatives by being the most widespread and found at the broadest range of elevations. While Sunken Button Lichen has apothecia that appear more recessed into the surface, Common Button Lichen's 'buttons' are notably raised and prominent. Other Buellia species in New England tend to be more specialized in their habitat requirements or have less pronounced reproductive structures.
